records.sourceFile: Reference Values for Hydration Biomarkers - Optimizing Athletic Performance and Recovery.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: The authors (who call it a narrative review) searched PubMed and Google Scholar for English-language, full-text, peer-reviewed field studies of adults up to May 2024, and accepted 16 that measured body mass change, urine specific gravity and thirst rating in competitions, training, weight-making and free-living days. Across the studies, body mass change correlated with urine specific gravity (r = 0.50, P = .013) and with thirst rating (r = 0.68, P = .001) in the pooled group means from Tables 1 and 2. The tables report pre- and post-exercise values, such as a 1.3% body mass loss with urine specific gravity rising from 1.019 to 1.023 and thirst from 2 to 5 in a 9-hour road cycling event.
records.limitations: The reference values are pooled group means from 16 small field studies (group sizes mostly 6 to 57), with different thirst scales, several studies missing standard deviations, and few combat sport data. Correlations are calculated from pooled group means rather than individual athletes.
records.synthesisCaution: The tables are averages from specific sports, climates and studies, so staff could read them as normal ranges or hydration targets for their own athletes when they are only a comparison point alongside individual baselines.

changes: tldr: 'Body mass change, urine specific gravity and thirst rating rise together' (body mass falls) -> urine specific gravity and thirst rose when body mass was lost ('all thirst ratings increased and all urine specific gravity values increased when a net body water loss occurred')
